newsitem.title: SPAIN: Papers said to show Spanish state's "dirty war" role.
newsitem.headline: Papers said to show Spanish state's "dirty war" role.

text.p: A Spanish newspaper published leaked government papers on Monday purporting to demonstrate that death squads which waged a "dirty war" against Basque separatist rebels in the 1980s were set up by the state.
Attorney General Juan Ortiz Urculo said the documents could provide evidence for reopening a high-level investigation into former government officials.
"We have to verify if they are authentic and if they are considered classified," he told state radio. "Each case has to be studied and re-weighed, but the road is open."

The Anti-Terrorist Liberation Groups (GAL) killed 28 people in 1983-87. Allegations that they were set up and funded by the state contributed to the election defeat last March of former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez's socialist government.

Supreme Court judges investigating the "dirty war" voted six to four last month against questioning Gonzalez, who denies involvement, but left the way open to reverse the decision if new evidence emerged.

The papers published in the pro-conservative El Mundo purport to directly demonstrate that GAL was set up by Spain's military intelligence agency CESID which also selected the first victim: alleged Basque rebel Ramon Onederra.
The courts are seeking the declassification of some 20 secret military intelligence documents that supposedly give details of the campaign of bombings, kidnap, torture and murder.
Ortiz Urculo said that in another case when secret papers turned up in public, the state prosecutors had recommended their declassification.
